title: Think of what you have
hookLine: count your best things and think how you'd miss them (Meditations 7.27)

cards: The power goes out for a day, and suddenly a light switch is a miracle. You get the flu, and for a week you'd give anything to taste food again.
A friend moves away, and the Tuesday coffee you took for granted becomes the thing you miss. What you have often gets noticed at the exact moment it's gone.
Marcus Aurelius tried to move that moment earlier, on purpose, while the lights are still on.

teach.b: In Meditations seven, twenty-seven, Marcus tells himself not to dwell on things he doesn't have as if they were already his. Instead, think of what you do have.
The mind easily runs to the gap: the bigger apartment, the better job, the life on someone else's feed. Marcus turns the head around.
From the things you have, he says, pick out the best ones, then think how eagerly you'd go looking for them if you didn't have them. That's the whole practice, and it's sneaky.
It uses the mind's hunger for what it lacks, and points it at what's already in the room: knees that work, the person who texts you good night, a quiet morning.

teach.h: HOW YOU'D SEEK THEM IF GONE.
teach.b: Picture them gone, and watch their value rise. Then the guardrail that makes it Stoic. Marcus adds a warning right away: don't get so attached to these things that you'd be thrown into turmoil if you lost them.
He isn't telling himself to cling.
Treasure them fully; hold them loosely. Other paths have their own practices of thanks, each with its own reasons.
What stands out in Marcus's version is that both halves come together: value what you have as if it were gone, and don't be shaken if it goes. Grateful and unafraid at once.

how: Readers of Marcus sometimes practice 7.27 by naming a few good things they have and imagining their loss, while reminding themselves not to cling.

o: a ruler who said to buy whatever might make you happy
a ruler who said to keep chasing what you still lack
the emperor who said to think of the best things you have

games.q: think of what you have — tap the pairs.
p: what Marcus says to pick out
don't be thrown if you lose it

s: Marcus says to cling tightly to what you have
he warns against being so attached that losing it would throw you into turmoil.
Marcus tells himself to think how eagerly he'd seek his best things if he lacked them

games.q: you catch yourself scrolling through someone else's life, wishing it were yours. what does Marcus's exercise suggest?
o: make a plan to get what they have.
pick the best things you already have, and imagine how you'd miss them.
games.why: Meditations 7.27: think less of what you lack, more of what you have, and how eagerly you'd seek it if it were gone, without clinging.

practice: Name three things you have that you'd miss terribly, a person, a body part that works, a place, a small daily pleasure, and take them one at a time.
Picture each one gone, just long enough to feel how you'd long for it, then let it come back, here, still yours today. Then loosen your grip, gently, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, whose exercise was to pick his best things and imagine seeking them if they were gone, without clinging to them. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: what I have. The best of it is already in the room. Day five hundred ninety-one, and the lights still on.
